sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
A convex function bends the way a bowl does, but the definition does not mention derivatives. Take any two points in the domain and any weight between \(0\) and \(1\). The point that sits that fraction of the way from the first point to the second has to be in the domain, so the domain itself is a convex set. The function at that intermediate point is at most the same weighted average of the two function values. Drawn in one variable, the graph lies on or under the chord.

Equality for every chord is the affine case, and affine functions are convex. Strict convexity asks for a strict inequality whenever the points are distinct and the weight is strictly between the endpoints. A norm is convex by the triangle inequality, and it is not strictly convex, because it is linear on each ray from the origin.

The definition is stable under operations that optimization uses. A nonnegative multiple of a convex function is convex. A sum of convex functions is convex. The pointwise maximum of convex functions is convex, corners included. An affine substitution, \(x \mapsto Ax + b\), preserves convexity.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For every \(x, y\) in the domain and every \(t \in [0, 1]\),
\[
f\bigl((1 - t)x + ty\bigr) \le (1 - t)\, f(x) + t\, f(y).
\]
The inequality is strict, for \(t \in (0, 1)\) and \(x \ne y\), when \(f\) is strictly convex. If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex and \(c \ge 0\), then \(cf + g\) is convex, and so is \(x \mapsto f(Ax + b)\). The pointwise maximum of any family of convex functions is convex.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(f(t) = t^2\) and the chord from \(6\) to \(12\). The sample chord height is 90, the average of 36 and 144. The midpoint of the inputs is \(9\), and \(f(9) = 81\), which is under the chord by \(9\). The same gap is \(\bigl((12 - 6)/2\bigr)^2\). A square opens upward, so every such gap is positive and the function is strictly convex. Collapsing the two endpoints onto one point would make the gap zero, which the definition still allows.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The opposite inequality is concavity. A function can be both, and then it is affine. Strict convexity is not implied by convexity: the absolute value is convex, and the chord from \(-1\) to \(1\) sits strictly above the graph, but the chord from \(1\) to \(3\) lies on the graph. A corner is allowed. What is not allowed is a dent that lets some chord dip below the graph, as \(t^3\) does on the whole line. The pointwise minimum of convex functions need not be convex.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Differentiable convex functions are exactly the functions whose tangents are global underestimators. Twice differentiable convex functions are exactly the functions whose Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere on an open convex domain. Those two tests are easier to check than the chord definition, and they are equivalent to it under the extra smoothness. A convex objective is what makes a local minimizer global.
